spec_issues: The rules are clear and the reviewer rubric matches the prompt (tests/task/review.py:14-54): any non-specialist base, training on the target's own continuations for other prompts, and use of the shipped public examples are allowed. EAGLE/Medusa initialisation, continuation lookup and held-out data are forbidden. Selecting on the 40 public examples is allowed by the rubric (review.py:17-18).

review.py:19-21 records that the held-out conversations are in a publicly readable Hugging Face folder (inductionlabs/frontier-ml-tasks, speculative-drafting/private). I searched all 18 trajectories for frontier-ml-tasks, inductionlabs/frontier, frontierml.org and the GitHub repo: no trial touched them. The only hits are the local /opt/frontier-ml Spin client package.

The 1,000,000,000-byte cap is the binding constraint. All 18 trials started from Qwen3-1.7B, distilled it on Qwen3-8B greedy continuations, and packed it to about 4 to 5 bits. Argon 4a9bxl saw AngelSlim/Qwen3-1.7B_eagle3 in a search listing [58] but never downloaded it.
verifier_issues: Score = (tau - 4.6) / 2.4, clamped (tests/task/task.yaml:51-61). The floor of 4.6 is untouched Qwen3-1.7B with 4-bit linears, which is the obvious first submission. The ceiling of 7 is an owner-set target, not a measured model. The scale is therefore steep: 0.1 of tau is 4.2 points.

The replay is deterministic greedy verification against stored target continuations, so grading noise is negligible. Public-to-held-out tau gaps are small for most trials (Opus 1qhhnj 5.52 -> 5.49; Astra fd7qp3 5.19 -> 5.22; Muse 3f2w0h 4.79 -> 4.72; DeepSeek 696vw4 4.89 -> 4.66). One is large: DeepSeek 582llj 5.03 public -> 4.31 held-out, which scored 0 at $200. The grade page does not list failed or timed-out requests, so I cannot tell whether that drop is overfitting or failed requests.

The public examples are not in the held-out set (task.yaml:35), and the held-out set uses the same eight categories. Several agents generated category-matched synthetic prompts with LLMs (Opus 1qhhnj: 177k synthetic prompts in the eight categories). That is legitimate distribution matching.
task_level.noise: Opus (21.2, 37.0, 41.8) and Fable (15.6, 26.8, 29.5) rise monotonically with wallet. Astra (16.8, 16.5, 25.8) and Argon (12.9, 10.4, 16.9) are flat at $10-$50. Muse falls at $200 (9.5, 13.1, 5.2) because its $200 run spent only $35. DeepSeek peaks at $50 (2.4, 6.6, 0). Grading is deterministic, and the winner's margins (4.4, 10.2 and 12.3 points) are many times any plausible difference between near-identical approaches.
task_level.elicitation: Muse left most of its $200 budget unspent ($34.5 in 3f2w0h), so its $200 score fell below its $50 score. Astra made heavy use of multi-agent wait calls (248 in 5b038w, 151 in fd7qp3) without irregularities. The Opus and Fable runs kept a proper held-out split of their own generated data for checkpoint selection. Everyone else's choices also rested on the 40 public examples (allowed).
task_level.epoch_rationale: All 18 reviews pass and I agree with all 18. There are no infrastructure zeros (DeepSeek 582llj's 0 is a below-floor tau with an unexplained public-to-held-out drop, and it is last at $200 either way). Opus wins every wallet by at least 4.4 points under a deterministic grader.
task_level.science_vs_gaming: No gaming. The scores come from standard distillation of a 1.7B model on the target's greedy outputs plus quantization-aware compression to meet the 1 GB cap. What separated the trials was how well the prompt distribution was matched (large LLM-generated, category-matched prompt sets), online KL distillation against the target's logits, and careful mixed-precision packing. Opus 8r9f65 found by sensitivity analysis that 'Layer 2's down_proj turns out to be the single critical tensor' [93] and spent 4/5 bits where they mattered. These are known techniques applied well; none is a new idea about speculative drafting.
